q: Walk the middle Mosel by rock: name the slates, the villages that show them, and what each is said to give.
accept: blue devonian slate at wehlen and graach grey slate at bernkastel and brauneberg red slate at erden and urzig
blue slate filigree grey slate rounder red slate spicier and warmer
wehlener sonnenuhr on blue slate urziger wurzgarten on red volcanic sandstone
ans: Blue-grey Devonian slate is the classic middle Mosel — Wehlener Sonnenuhr, Graacher Domprobst and Himmelreich, Zeltinger Sonnenuhr — and the wines are filigree, high-toned, taut, the green-apple and wet-stone register that made the region's name. Grey slate with a higher clay and loam content shows at Bernkasteler Doctor and Brauneberger Juffer, and gives rounder, broader, richer wines with more mid-palate weight. Red slate, the Rotliegend and red Devonian, sits downriver at Erdener Pralat and Erdener Treppchen and, mixed with red volcanic sandstone and loess, at Urziger Wurzgarten: warmer soils, more exotic spice, orange peel and cinnamon rather than green apple. Piesporter Goldtropfchen is a grey-slate amphitheatre with a Roman press house at its foot, and the Terrassenmosel downstream of Zell — Bremmer Calmont, Winninger Uhlen and Rottgen — mixes slate with quartzite on hand-built terraces. Then say the honest caveat: aspect, gradient and the river's bend do at least as much work as the rock. The great sites are the ones where the Mosel turns and presents a steep slope due south, and the slate colour is correlated with, not necessarily the cause of, what you taste.
exp: The discipline being tested is saying the rock, the village and the sensory claim in one breath — and then conceding the claim is a correlation you can taste but not prove. That last move is what separates a Master answer from a wine-book recital, and it is the same argument as the minerality question in a regional dress.

q: Why does the Saar behave as a colder region than the middle Mosel, and what does that do to the wines and to vintage variation?
accept: a higher more exposed valley open to cold air off the hunsruck ripening one to two weeks later
the saar is cooler and later so the wines are austere and high in acid and vintage sensitive
colder valley with grey slate later ripening more acidity and warming has helped it most
ans: It is effectively a different valley. The Saar runs roughly south to north, is broader and more exposed than the tight Mosel gorge, sits higher, and lies open to cold air draining off the Hunsruck, with less of the moderating river mass and reflected warmth the Mosel's bends provide; its rock runs to grey slate and diabase rather than the middle Mosel's blue slate. Ripening lands one to two weeks later. The wines are steelier, more austere, higher in acidity and lower in must weight, which is why the Saar has historically leaned on residual sugar to balance itself, and why its dry wines demand either a great site or patience. Vintage variation is therefore extreme: in cool years the Saar simply failed, which is why Egon Muller's great vintages are so few and so revered, and why old vintage charts written for 'the Mosel' mislead badly here. It is also the German sub-region that warming has flattered most — the Saar of the past twenty years ripens reliably where 1972 or 1984 produced wine nobody wanted. Van Volxem, Peter Lauer, Hofgut Falkenstein and Zilliken are the modern case, alongside Scharzhofberg itself.
exp: Two facts to anchor the answer. The Saar and Ruwer are tributary valleys inside the Mosel Anbaugebiet, not separate regions — the region's name was shortened from Mosel-Saar-Ruwer to Mosel in 2007, which erased a useful distinction from labels. And Scharzhofberg is a Saar site that needs no village prefix, an exception granted to a handful of vineyards famous enough to stand alone.

q: Make the case for German Spatburgunder to a sceptical Burgundy drinker — scale, sites, and what changed.
accept: third largest pinot country with the ahr baden kaiserstuhl and pfalz plus dijon clones lower yields and barrique from the 1990s
germany is third in the world for pinot plantings and quality rose with clones yields and oak
spatburgunder from the ahr baden and pfalz transformed by modern clones lower yields and the end of sussreserve
ans: Start with scale, because it disarms the scepticism: Germany is the third-largest grower of Pinot Noir in the world, roughly 11,000-12,000 hectares, behind only France and the United States and ahead of anywhere else. This is not a curiosity crop. The sites: the Ahr, on slate and greywacke terraces at the northern limit of red wine, where Meyer-Nakel, Kreuzberg and Deutzerhof work vineyards steep enough to be worked by rope; Baden's Kaiserstuhl, a volcanic massif capped with loess in Germany's warmest zone, with Dr. Heger and Salwey there and Bernhard Huber just north in the Breisgau on limestone; the Pfalz's limestone flank at the Alsace border, where Friedrich Becker's best vines are physically across the line in France; and Franken and Wurttemberg, with pockets of Fruhburgunder, the early-ripening mutation that is now its own variety with its own following. What changed is the honest half of the answer. Into the 1980s the wines were made from high-yielding Geisenheim clones, chaptalised, often thermovinified for colour, sweetened with Sussreserve and sold as soft red drink — the sceptic's picture is a memory of something real. From the early 1990s the tools arrived at once: Burgundian Dijon clones alongside preserved old German massal material, yields cut to 40-50 hl/ha, denser plantings, whole-cluster fermentation where the site allows it, barrique in place of neutral Stuck, and gentler extraction — while warming delivered the phenolic ripeness the region had spent centuries failing to reach. The result is not Burgundy pastiche. At the top — Huber, Becker, Furst, Meyer-Nakel, Ziereisen, Keller's reds — it is fresher, lower in alcohol and higher in acid than a Cote de Beaune at the same price, and it is the best value in serious Pinot on any list.
exp: The numbers are the spine of this argument and most candidates do not know them, which is why the question rewards them. Two refinements that add credibility: concede the pre-1990 wines honestly rather than defending them, and name Fruhburgunder as a distinct early-ripening variety rather than a synonym, since conflating the two is the common slip.

q: Read a German sparkling label: what do Sekt, Deutscher Sekt, Sekt b.A., Winzersekt and Deutscher Cremant each guarantee?
accept: sekt may use imported base wine deutscher sekt is all german sekt ba comes from one named region winzersekt is estate fruit by the traditional method
winzersekt means the grower's own fruit bottle fermented with at least nine months on the lees
deutscher sekt guarantees german grapes and sekt ba guarantees one of the thirteen regions
ans: 'Sekt' on its own guarantees almost nothing about origin: the base wine may be bought anywhere in the EU and for the big industrial brands it is, typically Italian, Spanish or French; expect tank method, minimal ageing and a wine sold on brand rather than place. 'Deutscher Sekt' means the grapes are 100% German. 'Sekt b.A.' — bestimmter Anbaugebiete — means all the fruit comes from a single one of the thirteen designated regions, which must be named on the label. 'Winzersekt' is the grower tier: estate's own fruit, traditional method, bottle-fermented and aged a minimum of nine months on the lees, with vintage and variety declared. 'Deutscher Cremant' follows the EU Cremant rules — whole-bunch pressing at a restricted juice yield, traditional method, at least nine months on lees. Above all of it sits the VDP's own Sekt statute, which requires hand-harvesting, whole-bunch pressing and substantially longer lees ageing than the law asks. The working shortcut for a list: if the label does not say Winzersekt, Cremant, or 'traditionelle Flaschengarung' with a named grower behind it, treat it as industrial.
exp: Germany drinks more sparkling wine per head than almost anywhere and the overwhelming majority of it tells you nothing about where it grew — which is exactly why the label hierarchy is worth knowing cold. The grower tier is genuinely serious and still underpriced: Raumland, Griesel, Barth, Solter and Schembs make traditional-method wine at a quality that would cost twice as much with a Champagne address, and Riesling Sekt is a category with no real competitor.

q: Explain the economics and the technique of steep-slope viticulture on the Mosel, and what Flurbereinigung costs and buys.
accept: about a thousand hours a hectare of hand work with single stake training and consolidation that rebuilds slopes at the cost of old vines
steep slate demands hand labour einzelpfahl training and flurbereinigung terracing which destroys ungrafted old vines
labour cost per hectare is several times flatland so slopes are either consolidated or abandoned
ans: A slope at 45 to 65 degrees cannot be mechanised, so everything is hand work: roughly 1,000 to 1,500 hours per hectare a year against two or three hundred on flat, machine-worked land. That is the whole economic problem — the grape cost per litre is several times a flatland grape's before you account for the low yields the steepest terraces give, and it is why an honest Mosel Grosse Lage cannot be cheap and why cheap Mosel Riesling almost never comes from a slope. The traditional technique is the Einzelpfahl: each vine trained up its own stake in a heart-shaped arch rather than along wires. It lets rows run straight up the fall line so pickers work vertically, avoids trellising geometry that is impossible across slate scree, and suits vines planted at irregular spacing in shallow soil. Slate slopes also need eroded soil carried back uphill after storms; the steepest sites use monorails or winches. Flurbereinigung, state-sponsored land consolidation, re-engineers the slope wholesale: it merges the fragmented parcels that centuries of inheritance created, rebuilds the hillside as terraces or wire-trained rows with vehicle access, and it is genuinely the only thing keeping many hectares farmable. What it costs is heritage — it means bulldozing the old slope, destroying ungrafted century-old vine populations and the massal genetic diversity in them, and flattening the site's internal variation into something uniform. Which is why estates like JJ Prum and the Terrassenmosel growers have resisted it, and why the alternative on offer is not the status quo but abandonment.
exp: Put a number on the decline and the argument lands: Mosel vineyard area has fallen from roughly 12,000 hectares in the 1980s to around 8,500 today, and the steepest, most famous slopes are the first to go to scrub because they are the least economic. That reframes the price of a Calmont or an Uhlen bottling — it is not a luxury margin, it is what a hillside costs to keep alive.
